name: Rafael Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Fairley Estate, on the beef side. We finish about four hundred bullocks a year and grow maize and grass to feed them. I'm on the feeder wagon at six, mixing silage and feeding the sheds, then bedding, then whatever tractor work there is. I've been there three years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is the tractor work in summer, cutting grass with the radio on, nobody bothering me. Worst is when a bullock gets out on the road, or when Pete the manager has me on the computer logging cattle movements, which I'm useless at. I'm still learning the stock side, if I'm honest. Pete says I've got good hands on a tractor and a lot to learn about cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe to the lads at the estate: told you, nothing changes. I don't go online about stuff like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, good. I've got a house deposit saved, about twenty-five thousand, and Lucy's doing well at the salon. Pete might get some help with the cattle movement paperwork, which means less of me getting it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Lucy and I would buy a house in the next year or two, somewhere near Fairley. I'd stay on the beef unit and try to learn the cattle side better from Pete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I like things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bed terrace in Ashby, the village by the estate, about ten minutes' drive. Lucy wants a garden, I want a shed. We've been looking for six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that bothers you already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Beef prices go up and down, but the estate is big and doesn't panic. If Fairley ever let me go, there are three or four farms within half an hour that would take a tractor driver.

say: I'd tell the lads at the estate **nothing changes**, and leave it at that.
I **don't go online** about things like this, so I'd say very little.
think: My **house deposit** of about £25,000 and Lucy's salon work keep us safe.
Pete might get help with the **cattle movement** paperwork I keep getting wrong.
do: Stay on the **beef unit** at Fairley and learn the cattle side from Pete.
Buy a **two-bed terrace** in Ashby with Lucy within a year or two.
feel: **Calm**, which is exactly how I like things.
S0.quote: If Fairley ever let me go, there are three or four farms within half an hour that would take a tractor driver.
fieldNote: He's **quiet and practical**, saying little and not posting online.
His life plan is a **house in Ashby** with Lucy, and AI barely touches it.
He knows he's **still learning** the stock side and is honest about it.

steps.text: Keep feeding and bedding the bullocks on the Fairley beef unit
Buy a two-bed terrace in Ashby with Lucy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who need to watch out, not us. Somebody's got to feed four hundred bullocks. I'd say that to Pete and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking AI would mostly mean Pete gets a computer to do the cattle records, and that's fine by me. The feeder wagon might go driverless one day, but slowly. I can't see it touching me for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep feeding the cattle and buy the house. If Pete wanted me to use some new app for the records I'd let him show me, but I'd rather he did it himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a flicker when I see a driverless tractor on the telly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen any of that kind of kit near you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm over at Ridgeway has a robot that pushes the feed up to the cattle in the barn, a little round thing. It's handy, I'll give it that. The robot at Ridgeway that pushes the feed up doesn't mix silage or calve a cow or get a bullock off the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a new app came for the records, why would you rather Pete did it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm slow with computers and I'd mess it up, and then Pete's got twice the work. I'm better on the tractor. Everyone has their thing.

say: I'd say the **office workers** need to watch out, not farm hands.
Somebody still has to feed **four hundred bullocks**, and I'd tell Pete so.
think: The thinking AI mostly does **Pete's records**, which suits me fine.
A **driverless feeder wagon** might come one day, but slowly.
do: Keep feeding the cattle and go ahead with the **house purchase**.
Let Pete handle any **new records app** rather than learning it myself.
Stick to **tractor work**, where I'm good, and leave computers to others.
feel: **Calm**, with a flicker when I see a **driverless tractor** on the news.
S1.quote: The robot at Ridgeway that pushes the feed up doesn't mix silage or calve a cow or get a bullock off the road.
fieldNote: He sees the scenario as **office work** first and feels safe on the tractor.
He'd **hand off** any new tech to his manager rather than learn it.
He's seen a **feed-pushing robot** nearby and dismisses it as limited.

steps.text: Keep feeding the bullocks on the Fairley beef unit
Go ahead with buying the Ashby house this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and nobody's ready, which would be true. I'd probably go quiet and listen to what others say first. I don't know enough to have a big opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. The thinking AI in 2028 runs the estate office and Pete's job changes, but the robots in 2031 take the feeder wagon, the tractor, all of it. I'd be thirty-one and all I know is tractors and a bit of cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house, honestly, because I wouldn't want a mortgage with my job going in three years. I'd keep the deposit in the bank and keep working. I'd probably wait and see what Fairley does before I did anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. I don't like not knowing what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucy about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucy we wait on the house, and Lucy would be upset, because she's been wanting a house for ages. Then she'd ask what happens to hairdressers, and I wouldn't know. Probably they're all right longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait and see. Is there anything you'd do in the three years before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe get my lorry licence, I don't know. But lorries would drive themselves too. I keep coming back to not knowing what to do, which is why I'd just keep working and save.

say: I'd say **nobody's ready**, then go quiet and listen to others first.
I'd admit I **don't know enough** to have a big opinion.
think: **Robots in 2031** take the feeder wagon and the tractor, all of my work.
I'd be **thirty-one** and know only tractors and a bit of cattle.
do: Put the **house purchase** on hold and keep the deposit in the bank.
Keep working at Fairley and **wait to see** what the estate does.
feel: **Sick** in my stomach, because I hate **not knowing** what's next.
S2.quote: I'd tell Lucy we wait on the house, and Lucy would be upset, because she's been wanting a house for ages.
fieldNote: The **house** is his first casualty; he won't take a mortgage with his job ending.
He has **savings but no plan**, and every idea runs into robots too.
He separates **2028 and 2031** clearly and sees 2031 as the end of his work.

steps.text: Put the Ashby house purchase on hold
Keep the £25,000 deposit in the bank
Wait to see what the Fairley Estate does

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people should calm down and think. Five years is a while. I'd say that to the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'd be thirty-five when the robots come in 2034. That's a long time to keep working, but at the end I'm still out. I'd probably buy the house and then worry about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with a smaller mortgage than planned, so it's paid down faster. I'd keep working and maybe ask Pete if the estate will train someone to look after the robots. I wouldn't do anything with AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd think about 2034 every time I paid the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you buy the house this time but not before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years is enough to pay a chunk off if we go small. I'd overpay every month. With two years' warning I'd be buying a house to lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Pete about robot training. Would you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate paid and it was hands-on, maybe. If it's all screens, no. I'd be honest with Pete about that.

say: I'd tell the lads there's **time**, so people should calm down and think.
I'd say **five years** is a while to sort things out.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** in 2034, and still out of work at the end.
I'd buy the house and then **worry about the mortgage** every month.
do: Buy the house with a **smaller mortgage** and overpay every month.
Ask Pete whether the estate will **train someone** to look after the robots.
feel: **Anxious**, thinking of 2034 every time I pay the **mortgage**.
S3.quote: With two years' warning I'd be buying a house to lose it.
fieldNote: The extra years change one thing: he'd **buy the house** but go smaller.
He'd consider robot training only if it's **hands-on and paid**.
He still expects to be **out of work** by 2034 and says so plainly.

steps.text: Buy a smaller house in Ashby and overpay the mortgage monthly
Ask Pete about estate-paid training for looking after robots
Keep working the beef unit at Fairley

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nothing to panic about. I'd say that and mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels long, but I know how fast three years at Fairley went. Robots in 2039, I'd be thirty-nine. I'd have to find something else at some point, and I'm not good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house as planned and keep working. Maybe in five years I'd look for a job that's less about driving, like hedge laying or fencing, which seems harder for a machine. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow kind. I'd mostly not think about it until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hedge laying. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Dennis on the estate does it in winter, laying the hedges by hand with a billhook, which is a big hooked blade. Every bend is different and you have to judge it by eye. I can't see a robot doing that well, though maybe I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not think about it until you had to. When would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see a robot doing my job on another farm, that's when I'd move. I know that's late, but that's how I am.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and nothing to panic about.
I'd mostly **mean it**, though not completely.
think: Three years at Fairley went fast, so **ten years** is less than it sounds.
I'd be **thirty-nine** in 2039 and bad at finding something new.
do: Buy the **house** as planned and keep working on the beef unit.
Learn **hedge laying** from Dennis in about five years as a fallback.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow way, putting it off until I have to face it.
S4.quote: When I see a robot doing my job on another farm, that's when I'd move.
fieldNote: He picks **hedge laying**, a craft he's seen, as work robots may struggle with.
He admits he'd **wait too long** to move, and accepts that about himself.
Ten years lets him **buy the house**, which is his main life goal.

steps.text: Buy the house in Ashby as planned
Learn hedge laying from Dennis in about five years
Keep driving and feeding at Fairley until robots arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years till the robots and no house and no idea. What would help is somebody telling me straight which farm jobs are safe for longest, and the estate paying for training on those.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what Lucy thinks. I keep saying she'd be all right, but I don't know that. I'd want her to have a say in all this.

headlineQuote: Three years till the robots and no house and no idea.
portrait: Rafael, 27, drives the **feeder wagon** and tractors on the Fairley Estate's beef unit.
He has a **£25,000 deposit** saved and plans a house in Ashby with Lucy, a hairdresser.
He **avoids computers** and would leave new apps to his manager, Pete.
He's calm while robots stay slow, but **alarmed** when AGI by 2028 puts robots on farms by 2031.
The **warning time** mostly decides one thing for him: whether to buy the house.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots in three years and no **house** or plan.
whatWouldHelp: Straight advice on which **farm jobs** last longest, plus **estate-paid training** for them.
